memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "However, if payment is demanded, the owner may redeem his life by the payment of whatever is demanded. This law also applies if the bull gores a son or daughter. If the bull gores a male or female slave, the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master of the slave, and the bull is to be stoned to death." - Exodus 21:30-32 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
These verses continue the case of the dangerous bull, allowing a ransom to be paid in place of the owner's life, and setting compensation even when the victim was a servant. The law refused to let any life go unaccounted for — including the servant's, valued here at thirty shekels of silver. Every person mattered enough to require a reckoning.

That figure, thirty pieces of silver, may stir something in you. Centuries later, this was the exact price at which Judas sold Jesus (Matt 26:15). The price once set for a servant's life became the price at which men valued the Lord of glory. What men counted as a small sum, God used to accomplish the redemption of the world. The Servant of all was sold for the price of a slave — and He willingly paid it to ransom us.

Here in Exodus, a ransom could redeem a guilty man from death. That whisper of substitution grows into a shout at the cross. We were condemned, but Christ gave His life as our ransom (Mark 10:45), buying back what we could never pay for ourselves. No sum of silver could match the true worth of what He gave.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
Do I grasp the staggering price Christ paid to ransom my life?
How should being "bought at a price" shape the way I live today?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord Jesus, You were valued at the price of a servant, yet You gave Your life to ransom mine. Thank You for buying me back; help me live as one truly Yours. Amen.
